summary: The paper adapts crosscoders (from cross-layer analysis) to cross-snapshot training-dynamics analysis of Pythia-160M and 6.9B, and uses them to (i) taxonomize initialization vs emergent features, (ii) attribute downstream task metrics (SVA, IOI, induction) to individual features via integrated-gradient attribution, and (iii) argue for a statistical→feature-learning phase transition supported by n-gram KL convergence and total feature dimensionality dynamics. It is a coherent, multi-angle interpretability contribution with a clear methodological novelty (using cross-snapshot crosscoder decoder norms as a proxy for feature strength across training) and non-trivial empirical observations (universal directional turning point around step ~1,000, complexity–emergence-time correlation, phase-transition signature). The main weaknesses are narrow empirical scope (Pythia only, single middle layer, small/relatively easy downstream tasks) and thin statistical treatment for several of the more evocative claims.
strengths: Genuinely novel adaptation: cross-snapshot crosscoders as a unified feature basis across pre-training checkpoints, with a principled argument for why decoder-norm ∥W_dec,i^θ∥ tracks feature presence over training.

Multi-angle analysis that reinforces itself: feature emergence curves, geometric turning point via cross-snapshot direction projections, and feature-complexity vs emergence-time correlation collectively tell a consistent story rather than resting on one metric.

Attribution-based circuit tracing on SVA/IOI/induction meaningfully connects microscopic features to macroscopic metrics; ablation experiments (remove top-k, keep only top-k) provide necessity/sufficiency evidence rather than pure correlation.

The statistical-to-feature-learning transition is supported with two independent signals (uni/bi-gram KL convergence approaching entropy floor + total feature dimensionality dip-then-rise), which is stronger than most single-signal phase-transition claims.

Well-scoped comparison against per-snapshot SAEs (Fig. 3) shows the crosscoder does not lose reconstruction/L0 quality despite the alignment burden — a critical control that pre-empts an obvious reviewer objection.
Limitations section is candid about Pythia-only scope, task simplicity, and discrete-snapshot cost.

key_concerns.issue: Empirical scope is narrow relative to the paper's framing about LLM pre-training in general. Only Pythia-160M and 6.9B are used, only one middle layer per model (L6 and L16), and no other architecture, tokenizer, or data-mix variation. Cross-snapshot claims like 'directional turning point around step 1,000' or 'statistical-to-feature-learning transition' cannot yet be attributed to LLM pre-training rather than to Pythia/SlimPajama specifics.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Repeat the core cross-snapshot crosscoder pipeline on at least one non-Pythia checkpoint family (e.g., OLMo, Amber, or Pythia trained on a different mix) and one additional layer per model; even a partial replication (e.g., decoder-norm evolution + n-gram KL) would substantially strengthen the generality claim. Alternatively, re-scope the abstract/conclusion to Pythia specifically.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical treatment of several headline claims is thin. The complexity-vs-emergence-time correlation is reported as Pearson r=0.309 on 100 LLM-scored features (a proxy prone to LLM-scorer bias); the 'universal directional turning point' is shown as a mean without dispersion in the caption; feature-lifetime and emergence-steepness distributions are described qualitatively. There are no seed-level replications of crosscoder training reported.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report confidence intervals / bootstrap CIs on r, and check robustness of the complexity score by using a second scorer model or by human spot-checking a subsample. Add dispersion (e.g., IQR bands) around the mean projection curve. Train ≥2 crosscoder seeds per snapshot family and show that decoder-norm trajectories and the directional turning point are seed-stable — this is the crux of the paper's evolutionary claims.

key_concerns.issue: Downstream-task evidence for the microscopic↔macroscopic bridge (Section 5) is confined to short, well-known toy tasks (SVA, induction, IOI) that already have small, well-understood circuits. This risks the interpretation that the method works precisely where the circuits are small and known, and undersells 'connecting features to downstream performance' as claimed in the contributions.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add at least one broader benchmark signal — e.g., attribute LM-loss or a compositional task (arithmetic, entity tracking, or a subset of BBH/MMLU tokens) to crosscoder features, even if the identified features are less clean. Alternatively, soften the contribution statement to 'we validate the method on classical circuit-tracing tasks.'

key_concerns.issue: The proxy claim 'decoder norm ∥W_dec,i^θ∥ reflects feature presence' is central but is only validated via a linear-probe sanity check deferred to Appendix C, and the reconstruction error term ε^θ(x) in Eq. 3 is not audited (i.e., how much of the metric attribution is being absorbed into the error term rather than into features).
key_concerns.suggested_fix: In the main text, quantify what fraction of the target metric’s gradient is captured by the feature-decomposition part vs the error term ε^θ across snapshots. If early-snapshot attributions live disproportionately in ε^θ, that is itself an important caveat for the 'no features exist early' narrative.

key_concerns.issue: The 'no features exist early / model only learns uni-bigrams' claim risks being partially tautological: if the crosscoder is trained jointly on all snapshots with a shared sparse code, early snapshots may lack sparse features because the training signal is dominated by later, richer snapshots — not necessarily because the underlying network has no structured representations at step 100.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Cross-check with a per-snapshot SAE on early checkpoints only (already trained in Fig. 3 comparison): do those early-only SAEs also find no non-trivial features beyond uni/bigram-like ones? If yes, the claim is much stronger; if no, temper the phase-transition framing.

key_concerns.issue: Related-work positioning against concurrent training-dynamics-of-features work (developmental interpretability, LLC/SLT-based phase transition detection, prior 'birth of features' analyses) is present but brief; the delta of this work vs. those is not sharply stated.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add 2–3 sentences explicitly contrasting: (a) the cross-snapshot crosscoder unified feature basis vs. per-checkpoint SAEs stitched via matching, and (b) the empirically observed dip-then-rise in total feature dimensionality vs. SLT-style predicted phase transitions.

questions_for_authors: How stable are the reported decoder-norm evolution trajectories and the 'directional turning point ≈ step 1,000' across different crosscoder training seeds and different λ_sparsity settings? Is the turning-point location a property of the model or of the crosscoder?

For attribution results (Fig. 7), what fraction of the metric’s gradient flows through the feature-decomposition term versus the reconstruction error ε^θ(x), broken down by snapshot? This is essential to know whether early-snapshot attributions are meaningful.

Have you compared 'features found by cross-snapshot crosscoder at final snapshot' against 'features found by a standard SAE on the final snapshot' beyond aggregate L0/EV — do the same concrete features (previous-token, induction, plural-marker) appear, and with matching top activations?

The complexity–emergence-time correlation uses Claude Sonnet 4 as scorer. Is the correlation preserved under a different scorer (e.g., a stronger or weaker model), and how much variance does scorer choice add?

Do you observe the same statistical-to-feature-learning transition when you train the crosscoder only on late checkpoints (say, step ≥ 1000), which would decouple 'the model has no features early' from 'the crosscoder was not incentivized to allocate features to early snapshots'?

For the SVA circuit, can you rule out that the identified feature set is essentially a re-discovery of previously mapped SVA circuits in small transformers, and if so, what is the added value beyond confirming the method works?
calibration_check: Claims are mostly appropriately scoped — the limitations section correctly flags Pythia-only scope and task simplicity — but the abstract/contributions still generalize to 'LLM pre-training' where the evidence is really 'Pythia pre-training at one middle layer'; the phase-transition framing in particular is stronger than a single-model-family study warrants.

significance.justification: Cross-snapshot crosscoders plus circuit-tracing across checkpoints are a genuinely useful addition to mechanistic-interpretability tooling; the interp community is likely to adopt and extend the approach.

novelty.justification: The methodological ingredients (crosscoders, attribution patching, SAE analysis) are pre-existing; the novelty lies in the composition and in framing decoder norms as an evolution proxy — a solid but not radical contribution.

rigor.justification: Method is sound and the core observations are supported by multiple independent measurements, but some load-bearing claims (e.g., decoder norm as feature presence proxy, no-features-early) rest on choices that are only partially audited in the main text.

statistical_soundness.justification: Limited quantification of variance: no seeds reported for crosscoder training, no dispersion around the mean projection curve, small-sample (n=100) LLM-scored correlation reported without CI; adequate for a workshop, thin for ICLR.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations section is candid about scope, task simplicity, and discrete-snapshot cost; the main overreach is generalizing Pythia-based findings to 'LLM pre-training' in the abstract and contributions.

clarity.justification: Overall readable and logically organized, but the extraction shows several muddled sentences and figure references (Fig. 2 vs Fig. 3, out-of-order placement), and the crosscoder equations use overloaded notation (aθ vs â^θ) that will trip readers.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard conference structure — Introduction, Related Work, Method, Analyses (§4), Circuits (§5), Phase transition (§6), Limitations, Conclusion — with ICLR-appropriate length and appendices for deferred material.

reproducibility.justification: Uses public Pythia checkpoints and SlimPajama, describes crosscoder architecture, loss, snapshot sampling, dictionary sizes, and evaluation tasks in enough detail for a competent reader to reimplement; missing pieces are seeds and precise λ_sparsity values but these can plausibly be inferred.

related_work.justification: Broad and accurate coverage across SAE/crosscoder, learning dynamics (NTK/IB/SLT), and circuit tracing; the delta vs concurrent developmental-interpretability and SLT-based phase-transition work could be more sharply articulated.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative, claim-supporting figures (Pareto frontiers, per-feature norm trajectories, direction-projection heatmap, KL and dimensionality curves), though the numbering/ordering in the extracted text is confused and several figures (esp. Fig. 4/5) would need dispersion overlays to be maximally convincing.

breadth_generality.justification: Two Pythia sizes, single mid-layer each, one dataset (SlimPajama), three toy downstream tasks; the claimed generality about LLM pre-training is not matched by the empirical breadth.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline accept: methodologically interesting and empirically coherent contribution to mechanistic interpretability, with real weaknesses in breadth and statistical rigor that a competent revision could address.
